claim_grade: Zelinsky's argument (EP violation even under rational-basis review): B-claim, Tier 1 recognised tax-law scholar, but unrefereed practitioner-journal/working-paper piece on a live question, origin of the argument only; 'unfairly stigmatizes' (SSRN/Crossref abstract wording): D-claim, his normative position, attribute only. Zelinsky is not listed in sources/audit/people-tiers.json (grep: zero hits), so judged by the section 4c rubric: tenured Cardozo professor of tax law, long record on state and local tax, so Tier 1 (not Tier 2 as the scanner says). Press items (Bloomberg Law via TaxProf/financial-planning): B-claim for litigation facts.
content_summary: Open text, with source of each claim. (a) Crossref abstract (SSRN deposit): 'In this article, Zelinsky argues that New York's pied-à-terre property tax surcharge on second homes fails to meet constitutionality requirements and unfairly stigmatizes ownership of expensive second homes.' (b) TaxProf Blog teaser (Tax Notes State text, no page locators): 'Judicial review of tax laws under the equal protection clause of the U.S. Constitution is limited. But even under this forgiving standard, New York City's pied-à-terre property tax surcharge on expensive second homes is unconstitutional because it violates the equal protection clause.' Published as 122 Tax Notes State 29 (5 Oct 2026); the SSRN item (8 pp, posted 9 Oct, written 5 Oct) is evidently the same piece. So the only ground evidenced is Equal Protection; Privileges and Immunities, Commerce Clause, uniformity, home-rule/enabling-act and stigma treatment are NOT confirmed from any open text; cited prior Zelinsky writings and the paper's added contribution cannot be stated (Crossref lists 0 references). Litigation context (Bloomberg Law via TaxProf, 5 Oct 2026): Ross/Wynn suit says the tax imposes 'discriminatory burdens on nonresidents and interstate economic interests' and, under US and NY constitutions, discriminatory classifications burdening the right to travel or lacking a rational basis; a second suit by Mastro for homeowners and a co-op corporation is described as similar. Those pending suits thus raise a rational-basis/equal-protection-type count that overlaps Zelinsky's ground, plus nonresident-discrimination/travel grounds not shown in his teaser. Staten Island Justice Wayne Ozzi's order (Monday, 10 Aug) took down the assessment roll pending an 31 Aug hearing; appellate judge Phillip Hom stayed it (Thursday, 13 Aug) pending decision whether the Appellate Division takes the case; about 17,000 notices; exemption deadline then 18 Sept (financial-planning.com/Bloomberg).

uncertainties: SCANNER PREMISES TO FLAG: (1) 'Academic Tier-2 source': wrong; Zelinsky is Tier 1 (recognised scholar) though the work is B-claim as unrefereed. (2) Scanner says the arguments include constitutionality plus 'stigmatizes' as if from the paper body; only the SSRN abstract says stigmatizes, the Tax Notes teaser says equal protection only. (3) 'Early legal challenges ... 10 Aug TRO reversed 13 Aug' is the page's framing; per Bloomberg/financial-planning the 10 Aug order was a Staten Island justice's order (Ozzi) in a suit that did NOT challenge the tax's legality (notice/assessment-roll adequacy), and on 13 Aug a single appellate judge (Hom) temporarily stayed it, not an appellate panel reversing it; the wiki sentence 'an appellate panel in Brooklyn lifted the order' overstates (the article says 'overruling a temporary restraining order' in its lede but the body is a judge's interim stay). Needs a check against the Mondaq source and a nycourts.gov docket before correction. (4) Wiki page says exemption deadline 6 Oct (extended twice); press says 18 Sept after the first extension from 21 Aug; consistent only if a further extension occurred; unverified here. (5) Wiki says the surcharge applies from 1 July 2026 and the scanner says effective 28 May; the wiki's Overview carries both ('took effect 28 May, applies from 1 July'), fine, but the frontmatter excerpt says 'took effect on 1 July'. (6) Scanner says SSRN was 'direct fetch bot-walled'; confirmed 403, not retried. (7) Article 30-C section text and any court decision were not openly retrievable (nysenate gave TOC only); the Oct 2026 constitutional suits (Ross/Wynn, Mastro) are not on the wiki page and are a more useful enrichment than Zelinsky alone; their press source is Bloomberg Law via TaxProf summary only. (8) Whether the SSRN 8-page paper differs from the Tax Notes version is unknown.
